title: Heat
lead: A soft drink and an ice cube set side by side end up at the same temperature, and no force acts through a distance while they do. This section defines heat as the energy that passes between them because their temperatures differ, separates heat from temperature, gives the joule, the calorie and the kilocalorie as its units, and follows Joule’s falling weights and turning paddles to the mechanical equivalent of heat, the work that produces the same effects as a heat transfer.
objectives: Define heat as transfer of energy.
summary_html:
• Heat and work are the two distinct methods of energy transfer.
  • Heat is energy transferred solely due to a temperature difference.
  • Any energy unit can be used for heat transfer, and the most common are kilocalorie (kcal) and joule (J).
  • Kilocalorie is defined to be the energy needed to change the temperature of 1.00 kg of water between $14.5^\circ\text{C}$ and $15.5^\circ\text{C}$.
  • The mechanical equivalent of this heat transfer is $1.00\ \text{kcal} = 4186\ \text{J}$.

figures.original_caption: In figure (a) the soft drink and the ice have different temperatures, T1 and T2, and are not in thermal equilibrium. In figure (b), when the soft drink and ice are allowed to interact, energy is transferred until they reach the same temperature T′, achieving equilibrium. Heat transfer occurs due to the difference in temperatures. In fact, since the soft drink and ice are both in contact with the surrounding air and bench, the equilibrium temperature will be the same for both.
Schematic depiction of Joule’s experiment that established the equivalence of heat and work.

exercises.prompt: Two samples (A and B) of the same substance are kept in a lab. Someone adds 10 kilojoules (kJ) of heat to one sample, while 10 kJ of work is done on the other sample. How can you tell to which sample the heat was added?

answer.solution: Heat and work both change the internal energy of the substance. However, the properties of the sample only depend on the internal energy so that it is impossible to tell whether heat was added to sample A or B.

exercises.prompt: An ice cube is placed in a cup of hot water. Which of the following statements correctly describes energy transfer at the molecular level?

options: Kinetic energy is transferred only from the hot water molecules to the water molecules in the ice.
Kinetic energy is transferred only from the water molecules in the ice to the hot water molecules.
Kinetic energy is transferred mostly from the hot water molecules to the water molecules in the ice.
Kinetic energy is transferred mostly from the water molecules in the ice to the hot water molecules.
answer.hint: Temperature measures the average kinetic energy of the molecules, and molecules on both sides of the boundary collide with one another. Ask whether every collision must send energy the same way, or only most of them.

exercises.prompt: The molecular description of heat transfer from higher to lower temperatures applies to ‘spontaneous’ processes, that is, processes in which no energy is added to or removed or from the systems by work or heat. Refrigeration is an example of work being done to remove energy from air within a given space, and thus lower the temperature of the air. Assume a typical kitchen refrigerator, where the air inside the unit forms the system with a temperature of $25^\circ\text{C}$, and the walls are kept at a constant temperature of $10^\circ\text{C}$. In terms of molecules and average kinetic energy, describe how the air is made colder.

answer.solution: The air inside the refrigerator is at a higher temperature than the walls, so its molecules have a higher average kinetic energy than the particles of the walls. When an air molecule collides with the wall, it gives up, on average, some of its kinetic energy to the wall, and so the average kinetic energy of the air molecules falls and the temperature of the air falls with it. This is heat transfer from the air to the walls, driven by the temperature difference. Left to itself the wall would warm as the air cooled, and the transfer would stop once the two reached the same temperature. The refrigerator prevents that by doing work: its motor removes energy from the walls as fast as the air delivers it, so the particles of the walls keep the same average kinetic energy and the walls stay at $10^\circ\text{C}$. With every further collision the air gives up more energy, and it goes on cooling until it too is at $10^\circ\text{C}$ and there is no longer a temperature difference to drive the transfer.

exercises.prompt: How is heat transfer related to temperature?

answer.solution: Heat transfer is caused by a temperature difference, and it goes from the object at the higher temperature to the object at the lower one. It continues as long as the two temperatures differ and stops once they are equal, when the objects are in thermal equilibrium. Temperature itself is not heat: temperature is a measure of the average kinetic energy of the atoms and molecules of a body, while heat is the energy that passes between two bodies because their temperatures differ, and a heat transfer changes a body’s internal energy and usually, though not always, its temperature.

exercises.prompt: Describe a situation in which heat transfer occurs. What are the resulting forms of energy?

answer.solution: Consider the soft drink and the ice cube of Figure 14.2, or a hot pan set down in cold water. The two objects are at different temperatures, so energy is transferred from the hotter one to the colder one until both reach the same temperature; that transfer is heat. The energy that leaves the hotter object was part of its internal energy, the kinetic energy of its atoms and molecules, and once it arrives it becomes internal energy of the colder object, raising the average kinetic energy of its atoms and molecules and so its temperature. If the colder object is ice at its melting point, the energy goes instead into changing its phase, as the next sections describe. In neither case is the energy stored as heat: heat exists only while it is being transferred.

exercises.prompt: When heat transfers into a system, is the energy stored as heat? Explain briefly.

answer.solution: No. Heat is energy in transit, the transfer that takes place because of a temperature difference, and once the energy has entered the system it is simply part of the system’s internal energy. A system has a well-defined internal energy, but it has no heat content, just as it has no work content: the same increase in internal energy could have come from heat transfer or from work done on the system, as by stirring, and nothing about the system afterward says which. This is why the book uses the phrase heat transfer, to emphasize that heat names a process rather than something a body holds.
